# Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots

Chalamalasetti Kranti ^(1,∗), Sherzod Hakimov ¹ and David
Schlangen ^(1,2) Address: 

###### Abstract

Collaborative robots (cobots) are designed to be safer and more
interactive than traditional industrial robots, share the same workspace
as humans, and assist them in a range of shop-floor tasks such as
palletization, joint assembly, and part inspection. Many of these tasks
involve repetitive workflows that may evolve with changes in production
environments and task specifications. These requirements motivate the
need for intuitive interfaces that allow workers to modify workflows on
the shop floor and generalise these routines for future use. This work
introduces the Teach-Abstract-Apply (TAA) framework, which enables human
operators to (a) teach new workflows to cobots in natural language, (b)
abstract the taught workflows into skills for later use, and (c) apply
these skills in different settings. As a case study, we apply the TAA
framework to a collaborative structure-building task and evaluate it
with both open-weight (Qwen3-Coder) and closed (GPT5.2-Codex) models in
self-play and cross-model configurations. Our results show that skill
abstraction improves task success rates and reduces interaction cost.
Beyond automated evaluation, a preliminary human-in-the-loop study
suggests that the pipeline also works with human instructions.

\helveticabold

## 1 Keywords:

collaborative dialogue systems, human-robot interaction, natural
language dialogue, skill learning, skill reuse, program synthesis

^(†)^(†)firstpage: 1

## 2 Introduction

Industry 4.0 ([Rüßmann et al., 2015](#bib.bib55); [Xu et al.,
2018](#bib.bib58)) suggests a transformation from conventional
automation to the use of smart machines and smart factories in
manufacturing. Its vision includes collaborative robots (cobots)
assisting human coworkers ([Colgate et al., 1996](#bib.bib4)) on factory
floors to enhance productivity, flexibility and efficiency. Unlike
traditional industrial robots, these cobots are designed with enhanced
safety mechanisms ([Wannasuphoprasit et al., 1997](#bib.bib59); [Akella
et al., 1999](#bib.bib10)) and simplified programming
requirements ([Stopp et al., 2001](#bib.bib60); [Estable et al.,
2002](#bib.bib61)) that enable them to work alongside human coworkers in
the same workspace and reduce the need for expert robot programmers in
operating them. However, real-world human-robot interaction is still far
from achieving such seamless collaboration ([Rodríguez-Guerra et al.,
2021](#bib.bib56); [Segura et al., 2025](#bib.bib57)). Various research
approaches ([Andersen et al., 2016](#bib.bib62); [Rosen et al.,
2020](#bib.bib63); [Schoen et al., 2022](#bib.bib64); [White and Mutlu,
2024](#bib.bib6)) have therefore focused on lowering the barriers to
using cobot interfaces. With many industrial robots deployed on assembly
floors, it is important to enable effective collaboration ([Aaltonen and
Salmi, 2019](#bib.bib78); [Sullivan et al., 2024](#bib.bib82)) between
humans and robots.

Recently, human-robot collaboration workflows have been improved by
advancements in large language models (LLMs) ([Zhang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib70); [Kim et al., 2024](#bib.bib12)), with a focus on
immediate, specific actions for _“here and now”_ scenarios ([Driess et
al., 2023](#bib.bib14)). These workflows usually operate by taking
commands from users ([Ichter et al., 2022](#bib.bib7)), with the backend
LLM analysing and reasoning about them ([Liang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib9)), preparing a step-by-step plan ([Huang et al.,
2022](#bib.bib13); [Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib11)) that considers the
current environment, and generating a program ([Singh et al.,
2023](#bib.bib8)) to perform the task. However, these methods focus
primarily on executing the current task rather than retaining and
reusing these behaviors, which is the core intent of teaching custom
behaviors to the robot. Furthermore, in industrial environments, it is
useful to teach a task as well as to capture the behavior so it can be
re-deployed in new settings with minimal user intervention ([Bauer et
al., 2016](#bib.bib79); [Villani et al., 2018](#bib.bib80); [Robots,
2024](#bib.bib81); [Sullivan et al., 2024](#bib.bib82)). Without a
mechanism to generalize and reuse learned behaviors, robots must be
re-taught or re-programmed each time the environment changes, limiting
scalability.

Teaching is often iterative, involving back-and-forth
clarifications ([Padmakumar et al., 2022](#bib.bib15)) and corrections
that lead to incremental refinement ([Chiyah-Garcia et al.,
2024](#bib.bib39)). Prior work on conversational programming ([Désilets,
2001](#bib.bib17); [Rahit et al., 2019](#bib.bib16)) addresses parts of
this process by enabling programs to be iteratively specified and
refined through dialogue ([Cypher and Halbert, 1993](#bib.bib18)).
Building on this, we propose the “TAA: Teach, Abstract, Apply” framework
that enables workers to talk to a robot in natural language ([Lauria et
al., 2002](#bib.bib19); [Gorostiza and Salichs, 2011](#bib.bib33)),
iteratively refine the workflow ([Thomason et al., 2019](#bib.bib21)),
and thereby teach new behaviors through a multi-turn dialogue ([Ge et
al., 2024](#bib.bib20)). As the name suggests, the TAA framework
consists of three stages: Teach, Abstract, and Apply. Teach refers to
the process of a worker engaging in a multi-turn interaction with the
robot, with the robot extracting relevant information from the
interaction. Abstract refers to the process of capturing and
generalising the extracted information into a behavior that can be
applied across different environments. Apply refers to the process of
applying these learned behaviors in different settings with minimal user
intervention.

![Refer to caption](2611.00297v1/TAA-TA_Overview.png)

Figure 1: Overview of the Teach and Abstract steps represented through
the structure building task in a simulated environment. Teach: the
worker uses natural-language to teach the Cobot an assembly arrangement;
Abstract: successful interaction traces are abstracted into a reusable
skill.

![Refer to caption](2611.00297v1/CLA-A_Overview.png)

Figure 2: Overview of the Apply step represented through the
structure-building task in a simulated environment. Reuse: refers to
using an existing skill at a new location; Repeat: refers to using an
existing skill with new properties — the washer color is set to ‘green’
and the skill is repeated across a set of locations in a pattern.

We test the TAA framework in a controlled setting through a
collaborative structure-building task (see
Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Introduction ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots"))
inspired by real-world industrial assembly scenarios, in which a worker
converses with the robot to build a structure in a grid-based
environment. These structures are composed of components such as
washers, nuts, screws, and bridges. During the Teach step, the worker
communicates the structure to be built in natural language in a
step-by-step fashion, and the robot semantically translates these
instructions into executable code. The outcome of the Teach step is an
interaction trace consisting of a set of instruction-action pairs, which
are then used by the Abstract step to capture and generalise the code
into a persistent function that can be adapted to different
environments. The Apply step focuses on evaluating how well the robot
can reuse these persistent functions in different settings without
requiring the worker to teach it again from scratch. To isolate the
effectiveness of this framework, the task is evaluated in a controlled
environment without a physical robot. An instruction-tuned Code LLM
generates executable code snippets for robot manipulation, which are
executed in a virtual simulator, thereby for now avoiding the perception
and control issues of a real robot.

With this controlled task setting, we investigate the following research
questions: (R1) Can LLM-based interpretation together with a dialogue
management framework realise acquisition of executable behaviours
through multi-turn natural-language dialogue? (R2) Can LLM-based
interpretation be used to abstract from the concrete teaching situation
a function that generalises to new spatial contexts and reused without
re-specification? (R3) Can learned behaviors improve task success and
reduce interaction cost compared to teaching from scratch? Our
contributions are threefold: (1) we present TAA, a dialogue-based
framework for teaching new behaviors grounded in executable programs;
(2) we introduce a behavior abstraction mechanism that generalises
demonstrated behaviors into reusable functions; and (3) we provide a
comprehensive evaluation, including reconstruction, reuse, and repeat
experiments, along with a pilot human study, demonstrating that learned
behaviors enable persistent reuse, reduce interaction cost, and improve
task performance compared to context-only conversational programming.

## 3 Related Work

To make cobots more accessible and make full use of their collaborative
potential ([Tsarouchi et al., 2016](#bib.bib69); [El Zaatari et al.,
2019](#bib.bib65); [Zhang et al., 2023](#bib.bib70)), prior work has
introduced a variety of interfaces, including text-based ([Karli et al.,
2024](#bib.bib73)), voice-based ([Ionescu and Schlund,
2023](#bib.bib71)), visual ([Kuhail et al., 2021](#bib.bib66); [Schoen
et al., 2022](#bib.bib64)), multi-modal ([Beschi et al.,
2019](#bib.bib68); [Fogli et al., 2022](#bib.bib72); [Lai et al.,
2026](#bib.bib74)), and kinesthetic teaching ([Ajaykumar et al.,
2021b](#bib.bib67)) interfaces. However, these interfaces primarily
support interaction for the current task. Our work extends such
interactions to generate persistent representations that can be reused
in later tasks.

### 3.1 Collaborative Dialogue Systems

Human-robot collaboration systems have evolved from instruction-only
style ([Lauria et al., 2002](#bib.bib19)) to interactive style ([Foster
et al., 2006](#bib.bib34); [Gorostiza and Salichs, 2011](#bib.bib33))
that showcases the necessity of back-and-forth negotiation. [Chai et al.
(2016)](#bib.bib37); [Chai et al. (2018)](#bib.bib38) discuss the
inherently ambiguous nature of human instructions, which motivates the
need for correction and clarification as core interaction
patterns ([Thomason et al., 2019](#bib.bib21); [Kane et al.,
2022](#bib.bib32); [Chiyah-Garcia et al., 2024](#bib.bib39)), the robot
must actively seek and incorporate feedback across turns. More
recently [Bonial et al. (2024)](#bib.bib35) explores establishing common
ground across different modalities of information in human-robot
dialogue. Although these systems advance collaborative interaction, the
knowledge learned through dialogue is not retained as an executable
representation. Our work builds on these systems by extracting and
persisting learned knowledge as reusable executable behaviors.

### 3.2 Conversational Programming

Prior work ([Heidorn, 1976](#bib.bib40); [Leggett and Williams,
1984](#bib.bib41); [Désilets, 2001](#bib.bib17)) proposed using
different modalities for translating natural language instructions into
programs. With recent advancements in LLMs, program synthesis has become
widely explored ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib42); [Austin et al.,
2021](#bib.bib43); [Hou et al., 2024](#bib.bib44)). [Nijkamp et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib45) explore multi-turn interactions for improving
overall program synthesis quality. Several works ([Huang et al.,
2022](#bib.bib13); [Ichter et al., 2022](#bib.bib7); [Liang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib9); [Singh et al., 2023](#bib.bib8); [Töberg and Cimiano,
2023](#bib.bib46); [Macaluso et al., 2024](#bib.bib48); [Kim et al.,
2026](#bib.bib83)) extend these ideas to generate executable robot tasks
and plans from natural language instructions. However, these works focus
primarily on context-bound execution and often assume users with
programming knowledge. Our work instead targets factory workers, who may
lack programming background but have domain expertise ([Aaltonen and
Salmi, 2019](#bib.bib78); [Bauer et al., 2016](#bib.bib79); [Villani et
al., 2018](#bib.bib80); [Sullivan et al., 2024](#bib.bib82)).
Furthermore, the outcome of the dialogue is captured as a persistent,
reusable skill representation in the form of an executable program.

### 3.3 Reusable Skills

Once deployed in the real world, collaborative robot routines evolve
over time, which traditionally involves re-programming ([Lozano-Perez,
1983](#bib.bib53); [Biggs et al., 2003](#bib.bib54); [Villani et al.,
2018](#bib.bib80); [Ajaykumar et al., 2021a](#bib.bib27); [Giberti et
al., 2022](#bib.bib26)). To reduce this burden, [Konidaris et al.
(2012)](#bib.bib50) proposed segmenting demonstrations into reusable
skill trees that allow users to build new sets of skills. [Lioutikov et
al. (2017)](#bib.bib51) learn a library of movement primitives using
probabilistic methods. Although these approaches aim to discover
reusable primitives from demonstrations, they still depend on physical
robot access and predefined model structures and representations.
Leveraging recent LLM progress, several works use them to generate robot
programs ([Mu et al., 2024](#bib.bib47); [Hu et al., 2024](#bib.bib49)).
[Wang et al. (2024)](#bib.bib11) demonstrate building a skill library
that allows reusing learned skills; however, the stored skills are
specialized rather than generalized. [Tziafas and Kasaei
(2024)](#bib.bib52) extend this to generalizable skills in lifelong
learning. Moreover, recent advances in coding agents have introduced
user-editable skills in text files with recipes for task development.
This has led to the evolution of an open-standard (SKILL.md ¹¹ 1
https://github.com/agentskills/agentskills) file that describes a skill
and its associated tools and workflows. Similar ideas have been explored
in robotics, to generate, refine and reuse robotic behaviors ([Lu et
al., 2026](#bib.bib75); [Hu et al., 2026](#bib.bib77); [Fu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib76)). While TAA shares the idea of maintaining persistent
skills with these works, it differs in how these skills are
systematically evaluated across different application settings through
reuse and repeat tasks. This is a necessary assessment because the goal
is not only to acquire a skill through teaching, but also to redeploy it
in new settings.

Taken together, these lines of research establish the building blocks
for TAA. Collaborative dialogue systems demonstrate the usefulness of
multi-turn interaction for clarifying and grounding user intent, but
they do not retain what is learned. Conversational programming shows how
natural-language interactions can be used to iteratively specify and
refine executable programs, but primarily focuses on generating programs
for the current task. Works on skill reuse demonstrate the value of
persistent, reusable robot behaviors, but does not evaluate how these
skills transfer under systematic task modifications. TAA brings them
together by enabling users to teach robots new behaviors through
multi-turn dialogue, abstracting the interaction into persistent
executable skills, and evaluating their reuse across systematic task
modifications.

## 4 Methodology

### 4.1 TAA: Teach, Abstract, Apply

Building on human–robot collaborative dialogue systems ([Foster et al.,
2006](#bib.bib34); [Gorostiza and Salichs, 2011](#bib.bib33); [Giberti
et al., 2022](#bib.bib26); [Kane et al., 2022](#bib.bib32); [Bonial et
al., 2024](#bib.bib35)), we formulate the Teach-Abstract-Apply (TAA)
framework as three distinct and sequential steps: Teach, Abstract, and
Apply, where the outcome of each preceding step provides input to the
next step.

The Teach step begins with a goal that is known only to the worker and
may be represented in different forms, such as an image (e.g., a
schematic diagram), text (e.g., a design document), voice note (e.g., a
description of the required functionality), or a combination of one or
more of these modalities. The worker interacts with the robot in natural
language and incrementally guides the robot towards the goal. The
interactions usually span multiple turns and include clarifications,
corrections and acknowledgments from both the worker and the robot. We
frame this interaction as a programming process which is refined
iteratively. The outcome of the Teach step is an interaction trace that
encodes the workflow. This is followed by the Abstract step, which
generates a persistent representation of the workflow. Necessary
information from the interaction trace is extracted and generalised so
that the retained representation can be extended to different
environments. The outcome of the Abstract step is a skill (e.g., a
program, a .md file etc.) that is available for later use. And the Apply
step follows, which applies the skills from the previous step in new
settings. The robot is equipped with these new skills and the evaluation
focuses on whether the skills can be adapted and applied to the new
settings (e.g., changing the attributes in a workflow, repeating the
workflow in different patterns, or building a new workflow using the
current workflow etc.) without teaching from scratch.

### 4.2 Structure Building Task

[Kranti et al. (2024)](#bib.bib3) proposed a structure-building task
(SARTCo) in which an instruction giver (Programmer) collaborates with an
instruction follower (Cobot) to reconstruct a goal structure, which
consists of different industrial-assembly-style configurations. The
Programmer receives the goal structure, represented on a $`8\times 8`$,
$`2.5D`$ ²² 2 A 2D grid with vertical stacking. grid, and instructs the
Cobot in natural language on how to reconstruct it. The grid is
represented as a Python array, and each grid cell can be accessed using
its row and column values, e.g., \[1,2\] or \[3,4\]. The Cobot
translates the instructions into code snippets, which, when executed in
a simulator, generate the resulting structure on the grid. They explore
generating first-order (primitive code) and higher-order (abstract
programs) programs from single-turn instructions. We use this dataset
for our experiments.

### 4.3 Realising TAA Framework

Our objective is to enable workers to teach robots persistent workflow
representations through natural language using TAA. For this purpose, we
instantiate TAA through the structure building task in a controlled
setting. We use instruction-tuned Code LLMs as both the Programmer and
the Cobot. The LLM powering the Programmer receives the goal structure
in textual form and instructs the Cobot in natural language. The Cobot
receives Programmer’s instruction along with the current state of the
reconstructed board in textual form and generates code snippets. These
code snippets are executed in the simulator, and the resulting structure
is returned to the Programmer in textual form as a follow-up response.
We use the clem:todd framework ([Kranti et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)) to
facilitate these interactions which follow a specific JSON schema (e.g.,
code, clarification, acknowledgment). At the end of the interaction, the
resulting instruction-code pairs are used to generate a higher-order
Python function that is saved as a skill. These saved skills are
evaluated for their extendability to new tasks. As mentioned in
Section [2](#S2 "2 Introduction ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots"),
we do not use a physical robot in this controlled evaluation.

#### 4.3.1 Teach: Teaching through Dialogue

A conversation demonstration (see
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.3.1 Teach: Teaching through Dialogue ‣ 4.3 Realising TAA Framework ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots"))
refers to an incremental teaching process through which the worker
teaches the cobot new manipulation routines for building a given goal
structure (also referred as a board). The Programmer may be a human,
LLM, or rule-based generator, while the Cobot may be a human or LLM, are
treated as the two players in the structure building task, and the Game
Master (GM) coordinates the turn-level interaction between them. The
task concludes when Programmer responds with DONE, or when the maximum
turn limit ($`15`$) is reached.

![Refer to caption](2611.00297v1/interaction_trace.png)

Figure 3: An example interaction trace showing how the conversation
proceeds. At Turn 1, the Programmer instructs the Cobot to place a red
screw on top of a yellow washer at position \[1,3\]. However, the Cobot
responds with an action that places only a washer and also uses the
wrong color. The Programmer corrects the color and proceeds with the
next step. At Turn 3, the Cobot asks for clarification about the screw
color, although it was already specified in Turn 1. In the next turn,
the Programmer repeats the details. The shared context shows how the
reconstructed board is updated after each Cobot action. When the
Programmer responds with DONE, the interaction is completed.

##### 4.3.1.1  Programmer: Instruction Giver

In line with existing work ([Chalamalasetti et al., 2023](#bib.bib22);
[Kazi et al., 2024](#bib.bib36)), we use LLMs to simulate instructors.
We conducted multiple ablation studies to design the final prompt
structure (details in
Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Ablation Studies ‣ 5 Experimental Setup ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots")).
Programmer is prompted ³³ 3 Refer to the Supplementary Material for
detailed prompts. in a zero-shot setting with information about the
environment, the task constraints, and the goal board to reconstruct.
The goal board is represented in textual format for a text-based LLM and
describes the stacking order and cell-level details, including the
occupied elements and their colors. Based on the ablation studies, the
prompt included a difference board, that shows the difference between
the goal board and the current reconstruction board for each cell and
stacking level. In the first turn, the difference board is None; in
subsequent turns, it is updated with the relevant differences.

When instructions are ambiguous or incomplete, Cobot requests
clarification, and Programmer elaborates or corrects the description. If
Cobot makes an error, such as placing unintended shapes in the grid,
colors, or spatial positions, Programmer provides corrective feedback so
that subsequent outputs align with the intended goal. Through this
iterative process, Programmer and Cobot collaboratively reconstruct the
goal board.

##### 4.3.1.2  Cobot: Instruction Follower

Cobot translates user instructions into executable code. We use
instruction-tuned code LLMs for this purpose. Cobot is prompted with
information about the environment, the task constraints, and the current
state of the reconstruction board. Similar to Programmer, the current
reconstruction board is represented in textual format, describing the
stacking order and cell-level details, including the occupied elements
and their colors.

For a given input instruction, Cobot is expected to either produce the
corresponding action sequence (e.g.,, input: “place a red washer in cell
4,3”; output: put(board, ‘washer’, ‘red’, x=4, y=3)) or ask for
clarification (e.g.,, “there is already a nut present in the same
location. do I need to remove the nut before placing a washer or stack
on it?”). The generated action sequences are executed in a virtual
simulator. If execution fails, Cobot receives feedback about the error
and either corrects the code or asks for clarification when the error
cannot be resolved without additional context from Programmer. If
execution continues to fail after three attempts, the interaction is
terminated and the test instance is treated as a failure. Cobot can also
acknowledge Programmer queries (e.g.,, input: “do you know how to place
a washer?”; output: “Yes, I know!”).

##### 4.3.1.3  Game Master: Interaction Coordinator

The Game Master (GM) manages the turn-level interaction between
Programmer and Cobot. At the beginning of each turn, GM provides
Programmer with the goal board and the difference board. Programmer then
gives a natural language instruction to guide the reconstruction, and
Cobot responds by translating the instruction into executable Python
code, asking for clarification, or providing an acknowledgment when
appropriate. GM validates each player response to ensure that it follows
the required format; if a response does not satisfy the format
requirements, the interaction is aborted. GM also executes Cobot’s
generated code in the virtual simulator and shares the updated
reconstruction board with both players in the subsequent turn. When
execution fails, GM forwards the error to Cobot, which can revise the
code or ask Programmer for clarification. The interaction continues
until Programmer responds with DONE, the maximum turn limit ($`15`$) is
reached, or execution fails after three attempts. Once Programmer
responds with DONE, GM evaluates task success by comparing the
reconstructed board with the goal board at each cell location, including
component color and stacking order. If the reconstruction is successful,
GM forwards the instruction-code pairs, consisting of each Programmer
instruction and its corresponding Cobot-generated action, to the
Optimizer module for further processing. The prompt structure, number of
execution retries, and overall task interaction are based on the
ablation studies, discussed in
Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Ablation Studies ‣ 5 Experimental Setup ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots").

#### 4.3.2 Abstract (Optimizer): Generalisable Function Generator

Only successful reconstruction interactions are used for optimization,
since they correspond to cases where the goal board was reconstructed
correctly. Unsuccessful or incorrect interactions are excluded.
Optimizer receives the sequence of instruction-response pairs collected
during reconstruction, where each Programmer instruction is paired with
the corresponding Cobot-generated action as shown in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.3.2 Abstract (Optimizer): Generalisable Function Generator ‣ 4.3 Realising TAA Framework ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots").

![Refer to caption](2611.00297v1/CLA_Optimization.png)

Figure 4: Overview of reusable function generation. Given the
instruction-response pairs and a predefined function signature, the Code
LLM abstracts the primitive code snippets into a reusable higher-order
function. The generated function is then evaluated by comparing the
structure it reconstructs with the structure produced by the input code
snippets, evaluating each cell for component type, color, and stacking
level.

The Cobot output contains primitive placement sequences and may also
reflect clarifications or corrections made during the interaction.
Although these sequences are sufficient to reconstruct the goal board,
they cannot be reused in later tasks unless they are converted into a
reusable representation. We therefore abstract recurring action patterns
into higher-order Python functions that produce the same goal board
state as the primitive code sequences.

Optimizing code into reusable abstractions is often time-consuming and
requires human expertise. Prior work ([Yang et al., 2023](#bib.bib24);
[Tapia et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Cynthia, 2025](#bib.bib25)) has shown
that LLMs can support optimization processes. Building on this, we
follow a similar LLM-as-optimizer paradigm and use an instruction-tuned
code LLM to iteratively transform the generated code into a reusable
skill function. The optimizer is queried in a zero-shot setting with a
prompt that includes information about the environment, task
constraints, and instruction-response pairs from the reconstruction
task. The output is a Python function, referred to as a skill, that
encapsulates the manipulation routine in a reusable form for subsequent
tasks.

The optimizer receives the full sequence of instruction-response pairs
without pre-processing (see
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.3.2 Abstract (Optimizer): Generalisable Function Generator ‣ 4.3 Realising TAA Framework ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots")).
Since the sequence may include instructions that correct or clarify
earlier ones, the optimizer is prompted to read the entire interaction,
identify which code reflects the final intended actions, and discard any
code that was later replaced or fixed. For example, an instruction may
place a washer using put(board, ‘washer’, ‘red’, x=1, y=3). If a later
instruction corrects the washer color to yellow with put(board,
‘washer’, ‘yellow’, x=1, y=3). The final code used for optimization
would therefore include only put(board, ‘washer’, ‘yellow’, x=1, y=3).
The prompt also instructs the optimizer to follow a predefined function
signature. For illustration, a generated skill may be defined as def
\<object_name\>(board, colors, x, y) and be used as ws(board,
\[‘yellow’, ‘red’\], 1, 3). The generated function can then be stored
and reused in subsequent tasks
(Sections [4.3.3.1](#S4.SS3.SSS3.P1 "4.3.3.1 Reuse: Systematic Evaluation of Skill Generalisability ‣ 4.3.3 Apply ‣ 4.3 Realising TAA Framework ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots")
and
[4.3.3.2](#S4.SS3.SSS3.P2 "4.3.3.2 Repeat: Systematic Evaluation of Repeated Skill Use ‣ 4.3.3 Apply ‣ 4.3 Realising TAA Framework ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots")).

For a given input, Optimizer is expected to generate a Python function
that produces the same board state as the input primitive code sequences
when executed in the virtual simulator. Equivalence is determined by
comparing the final board states produced by the generated function and
the primitive code sequences. If the Optimizer output fails to execute,
it receives feedback about the error and can revise the code. If it
cannot correct the error within three attempts, the task is aborted and
the test instance is treated as a failure. The task is considered
successful when the Optimizer output replicates the board state and is
considered failed when the maximum turn limit ($`10`$) is reached.

#### 4.3.3 Apply

##### 4.3.3.1  Reuse: Systematic Evaluation of Skill Generalisability

Once cobots are deployed in the real world, onsite requirements may
differ from their pre-programmed routines due to customization needs or
changing task constraints. These changes can include a new product
variant, a change in assembly geometry, such as a V-shape instead of a
T-shape, or an added inspection step, such as checking alignment before
fastening. Adapting to such changes often requires a programming
expert ([Ajaykumar et al., 2021a](#bib.bib27); [Giberti et al.,
2022](#bib.bib26)) or the use of complex interfaces ([Akkaladevi et al.,
2019](#bib.bib28); [Dmytriyev et al., 2022](#bib.bib29); [George et al.,
2023](#bib.bib5); [Ayalew et al., 2025](#bib.bib30)), which can be
costly ([Barravecchia et al., 2023](#bib.bib31)) and slow ([Ajaykumar et
al., 2021a](#bib.bib27)).

We design the reuse task to study whether skills generated by the
Optimizer can be adapted under controlled modifications. Specifically,
we evaluate changes in color and spatial information, reflecting
incremental adjustments common in assembly workflows. We are interested
in: (a) can the model identify the required skill from the list of
available skills? and (b) can the model use the selected skill with the
correct modifications for the new requirement?

Similar to reconstruction, the reuse task consists of two players,
Programmer and Cobot, interacting over a multi-turn dialogue to
replicate a goal board. The skills generated by the Optimizer are made
available in Cobot’s context. Each skill is represented by its function
signature and a single-line description of the object it builds.
Programmer is prompted to ask whether Cobot is aware of the relevant
skill before guiding it to build the modified object using the available
skills. Cobot is expected to identify the relevant skill from its
context and generate a function call with the correct arguments. This
function call is executed in the virtual simulator using the
corresponding skill definition learned during optimization. If the
corresponding skill is not available in the library, we use the ground
truth function definition to execute the function call.

If Cobot cannot identify a suitable skill, Programmer provides
step-by-step instructions, and the interaction falls back to the Teach
reconstruction loop. The task is completed when Programmer signals
completion or when the maximum turn limit ($`15`$) is reached. Once
Programmer responds with DONE, GM evaluates task success by comparing
the reconstructed board with the goal board at each cell location,
including component color and stacking order.

##### 4.3.3.2  Repeat: Systematic Evaluation of Repeated Skill Use

As robots are often used for repetitive tasks, we extend our study to
examine how learned skills generalize to goal boards with repeated
spatial patterns. The repeat task consists of goal boards where a single
object is repeated across the grid in different patterns. Similar to the
reuse
task [4.3.3.1](#S4.SS3.SSS3.P1 "4.3.3.1 Reuse: Systematic Evaluation of Skill Generalisability ‣ 4.3.3 Apply ‣ 4.3 Realising TAA Framework ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots"),
the objects used in the goal boards are modified versions of the skills
generated by the Optimizer. In the repeat task, these objects are placed
multiple times across the board in structured patterns, requiring the
models to recognize and generalize the repetition. We are interested in:
(a) whether the models can identify the correct repetition pattern,
including spatial arrangement, order, and frequency, to accurately
replicate it; and (b) whether the models can express this pattern using
appropriate programming abstractions, such as loops or nested loops.

The repeat task follows the same two-player, multi-turn interaction as
the reuse task. Cobot is equipped with the learned skill set and is
expected to select the relevant skill, generate the corresponding
function calls, and use suitable programming abstractions to place the
object repeatedly across the grid. If Cobot cannot identify a suitable
skill, Programmer provides step-by-step instructions, and the
interaction falls back to the Teach reconstruction loop. The task is
completed when Programmer responds with DONE or when the maximum turn
limit ($`30`$) is reached. Once Programmer responds with DONE, GM
evaluates task success by comparing the reconstructed board with the
goal board at each cell location, including component color and stacking
order.

## 5 Experimental Setup

As the TAA framework follows two-player interaction, both players are
prompted in a zero-shot setting and receive the full interaction history
at every turn. More details about the prompt context are available in
the Supplementary Material.

### 5.1 Dataset

To evaluate the proposed approach, we require an environment that mimics
a manipulation setting and allows collaboration over multiple turns. The
tasks also require semantic representations expressed in code so that
outputs can be evaluated objectively. We use the SARTCo ([Kranti et al.,
2024](#bib.bib3)) dataset for our experiments. The SARTCo dataset is an
8$`\times`$8 2.5D (a two-dimensional grid with vertical stacking)
grid-world environment in which objects are arrangements of connected
components of nuts, washers, screws, and bridges. A grid containing one
or more such objects is referred to as a board. For the reconstruction
and reuse tasks, the goal boards contain single objects, whereas the
repeat task uses goal boards with multiple objects. Since the publicly
released dataset contains a limited number of test samples ($`130`$), we
generated a new set of samples using the same framework, producing a
training set of 165 samples and validation and test sets of 495 samples
each. The training set is used in the reconstruction task for teaching
the skills. The validation and test sets contain three instances (that
differ in colors and locations) for each of the $`165`$ unique skills in
the training set without any overlap. This setup is designed to evaluate
whether the learned skills can generalize to unseen variations.

### 5.2 Ablation Studies

We conducted multiple ablation studies to design the prompt. This
required several design decisions, including the number of turns before
stopping the interaction, whether the cobot should ask clarification
questions, whether execution error feedback improves reconstruction and
overall success, and the number of turns allowed for the optimization
step. Together, these decisions determine our final configuration. The
detailed ablation results are available in the supplementary material.

### 5.3 Evaluation with a Human Programmer

To evaluate the performance of the proposed pipeline under natural human
instructions, we conducted a preliminary human-in-the-loop evaluation on
a subset of the test set. We randomly selected 50 test instances (seed = 76) and employed a human participant as the Programmer, while the Cobot
was evaluated on the reuse and repeat tasks. In these experiments, the
Cobot was powered by Qwen3-Coder using the skill-set generated by
Qwen3-Coder. The participant was a student assistant in the department
who was familiar with the experimental setup but had not worked on this
paper.

### 5.4 Model Selection

We experiment with both an open-weight model (Qwen3 Coder 30B A3B
Instruct ⁴⁴ 4
[https://qwen.ai/blog?id=qwen3-coder](https://qwen.ai/blog?id=qwen3-coder))
and a closed model (GPT5.2-Codex ⁵⁵ 5
[https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.2-codex](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.2-codex)).
These models were chosen based on their competitive performance on code
generation benchmarks, representing both open-weight and closed model
paradigms. We also investigate whether our approach can be realised with
an open-weight model that can potentially be self-hosted and has latency
advantages, by comparing it to a proprietary model that incurs
usage-based costs. Hence as a case-study, we evaluate one model from
each paradigm. The experiments include using the same model for both the
Programmer and the Cobot, as well as cross-model pairings (using
GPT5.2-Codex as the Programmer and Qwen3-Coder as the Cobot, and vice
versa). The rationale for the cross-model pairings is to understand the
sensitivity of the Cobot to the choice of the Programmer and its impact
on task success. The open-weight model is hosted locally on a single
A100 GPU and is accessed through a local API endpoint. The closed model
is accessed via Azure APIs. Both models are run with a temperature of
$`0`$ to reduce output variance, with a max_new_tokens limit of $`1000`$
for reconstruction and reuse tasks and $`2000`$ for the repeat task.

### 5.5 Evaluation Metrics

As the dataset provides a known target configuration along with its
semantic representation, we conduct a detailed evaluation of the model
responses.

Reconstruction task: We use execution success to compare the
reconstructed board state with the goal board in terms of the occupied
cells (element type, color, location, and stacking order). In addition,
we compute dialogue-level metrics, including success rate and
clarification and correction rates normalized by the number of elements
in the object, and the number of turns required to complete the
reconstruction.

Optimization task: We use execution success to compare the board state
produced by the generated optimized function with the goal board in
terms of the occupied cells, measuring optimization accuracy. We also
compute several structural metrics using Python’s abstract syntax tree
(AST), including whether the generated code contains a valid function
definition, the reduction in put calls relative to the input, and the
presence of loops indicating abstraction rather than repetition. We
further measure the bytecode length before and after optimization using
Python’s dis module to assess structural compression.

Reuse and Repeat tasks: For the reuse and repeat tasks, we use execution
success to compare the generated board with the ground truth board in
terms of the occupied cells (element type, color, location, and order),
measuring task accuracy when using learned skills. In addition, we
measure the rate at which the model selects the correct function from
the available skill set and the rate at which it applies this function
with the correct arguments. We also compute the token-based cost for
both No-skills and Skills-Used settings across self-play and cross-model
pairings, analysing the trade-off between task success and computational
cost.

## 6 Results

We present our results based on the research questions presented in
Section
[2](#S2 "2 Introduction ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots"),
covering the talk–teach interaction, skill generation through
optimization, and the reuse, repeat of learned skills in new contexts,
providing both quantitative and qualitative analysis.

| Model        | Success Rate   |              |         | Token Cost (\$) |
|              | Reconstruction | Optimization | Overall |                 |
| Qwen3-Coder  | 0.69           | 0.93         | 0.64    | 1.41            |
| GPT5.2-Codex | 0.93           | 1.00         | 0.93    | 10.43           |

Table 1: Performance comparison between Qwen3-Coder and GPT5.2-Codex on
reconstruction and optimization tasks, reporting success rates for each
component and overall performance along with token cost; Overall =
Reconstruction x Optimization success; Token cost is the total across
all test instances.

### 6.1 Reconstruction Task

Can we through this methodology teach new behaviors through multi-turn
natural language dialogue? This question examines the teach stage of the
TAA pipeline, where the Cobot learns to reconstruct a goal board through
multi-turn dialogue with the Programmer.

Table [1](#S6.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 6 Results ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots")
shows the success rate of teaching new skills. We first compute the
reconstruction success rate, where the Programmer collaborates with the
Cobot to accurately reconstruct the board while generating the primitive
code snippets. The results show that reconstruction success is higher
for the closed model (GPT5.2-Codex) than for the open-weight model
(Qwen3-Coder). Some of the failures in Qwen3-Coder are due to the model
repeatedly responding with ‘‘Yes, I know’’ without generating code
snippets, or continuing to ask clarification questions without
correcting misplacements caused by using the wrong colors or incorrect
locations. Although reconstruction success varies between the models,
both models show higher optimization success rates for successful
reconstructions. The token cost is computed based on the number of
tokens used and pricing information from OpenRouter⁶⁶ 6
[https://openrouter.ai/](https://openrouter.ai/), and is reported for
reference only⁷⁷ 7 Qwen3-Coder is hosted on a local GPU; however, the
token price is computed to show comparison with commercial model usage.
as pricing is subject to change by API providers.

Figure 5: Performance of Qwen3-Coder and GPT5.2-Codex as task complexity
increases (measured by the number of elements per object). The plots
show average number of clarification and correction turns, and overall
success rate for reconstruction task with varying structural complexity.

These results indicate that it is possible to acquire new executable
behaviors through the proposed framework, and that the success rate
depends on the model’s capabilities. We now examine the performance
drops through the lens of object complexity and how it affects
interaction behavior and reconstruction success. Specifically, we
analyze how the success rate changes with the number of elements in the
object, and whether clarification and correction rates change with
increasing object complexity.
Figure [5](#S6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 6.1 Reconstruction Task ‣ 6 Results ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots")
shows that for Qwen3-Coder, clarifications and corrections appear to
increase with the number of elements. In contrast, GPT5.2-Codex shows an
almost flat trend in clarifications and only a few instances of
corrections for objects with four elements, while all other cases show
zero corrections. For both models, the reconstruction success rate
declines as the number of elements in the object increases. The drop is
higher for Qwen3-Coder, whereas GPT5.2-Codex appears less affected,
although a slight decrease is still observed.

#### 6.1.1 Abstract: Reusable Function Generation

After a successful Teach step, we now proceed with the Abstract step, to
abstract the primitive action sequences. We evaluate how accurately
models can abstract the given code snippets into a higher-order
function.

Figure 6: Success rate of Qwen3-Coder and GPT5.2-Codex on code
optimization objectives. Each point represents the proportion of test
instances where the model correctly applied the required transformation,
including using correct function names, using loop constructs, reducing
put() calls, and minimizing output byte length; Vertical lines connect
the two models scores to highlight the gap.

Table [1](#S6.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 6 Results ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots")
shows that both the models achieve higher optimization rates. That
indicates the abstracted functions reproduce the behavior of the input
primitive sequences. We next analyse how well these functions are
structurally optimized. This question is important as the goal is not
only successful reconstruction but also generating a function that is
both optimized and reusable, capable of reproducing the learned behavior
in new contexts.
Figure [6](#S6.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 6.1.1 Abstract: Reusable Function Generation ‣ 6.1 Reconstruction Task ‣ 6 Results ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots")
shows the analysis across model configurations.

We first check whether the output contains a valid function definition
with the correct object name. We then examine how the primitive
sequences are structured within the generated function. As the input
consists of multiple put() calls, recurring patterns may be present, and
an effective optimizer should abstract such patterns. We therefore
evaluate whether a loop is present in the generated output and whether
the overall number of put() calls is reduced, since loop alone does not
guarantee correct abstraction. Finally, we compute whether the bytecode
length is reduced after optimization. Both models consistently generate
the correct function signature. GPT5.2-Codex effectively uses loops and
reduces the number of put() calls, while Qwen3-Coder shows competitive
performance on both metrics. However, neither model shows a significant
reduction in bytecode length, although GPT5.2-Codex performs slightly
better. This is because Python’s loop constructs and data structures
such as list definitions, zip, and tuple unpacking introduce compilation
overhead that can offset or exceed the savings from fewer put() calls.
Overall, this shows that the optimizer able to abstract the code that is
not only functionally correct but also structurally optimized.

Taken together, the results suggest that Teach and Abstract steps enable
the acquisition of new executable behaviors through multi-turn
natural-language dialogue and their abstraction into reusable skills.
The generalisability of these abstracted skills is further evaluated
through the reuse and repeat tasks.

### 6.2 Reuse

With the generation of reusable skills, the next step is to evaluate
whether these skills can be applied in new scenarios. We evaluate three
settings: the test set without any skills (no-skills), which effectively
reduces the reuse task to a reconstruction-style test and acts as the
baseline; the test set using the skill set learned by Qwen3-Coder (Qwen
skills); and finally using the skill set learned by GPT5.2-Codex (Codex
skills). This allows us to study the impact of having learned skills on
overall task success and associated cost. We additionally evaluate
cross-pairings of the models to examine whether the choice of Programmer
(instruction giver) influences the Cobot (instruction follower) model.
In cases where a corresponding skill is unavailable, as not all
reconstruction instances are successful, these instances fall back to
the reconstruction-style task.

![Refer to caption](2611.00297v1/reuse_stats.png)

Figure 7: Cost–performance trade-off for the reuse task. Each point
represents a model configuration, comparing success rate and token cost
when responses are generated without skills, with Qwen skills, or with
Codex skills; G-Q, Q-Q etc. Labels denote Programmer–Cobot pairs; G-Q:
GPT as Programmer and Qwen as Cobot; Q-G: Qwen as Programmer and GPT as
Cobot; The y-axis is truncated to the range 0.6-1.0 to highlight
differences among performance scores.

Impact of Skill Usage: As shown in
Figure [7](#S6.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 6.2 Reuse ‣ 6 Results ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots"),
using learned skill sets improves task success compared to the no-skill
baseline. For the Qwen3-Coder Cobot using the same model as programmer
(Q–Q), the success rate increases from 0.72 without skills to 0.86 when
using the Qwen3-Coder skill set and to 0.87 when using the GPT5.2-Codex
skill set. When the programmer is changed to GPT5.2-Codex (G–Q), the
success rate increases to 0.99 for both skill sets (Qwen3 skills: 0.99;
Codex skills: 0.99). We further observe that using skill sets reduces
overall token cost compared to the no-skill baseline. Without skills,
the cost is \$3.63 for Q–Q and \$7.96 for G–Q. With skill reuse, the
cost becomes \$2.64 for Q–Q and \$4.88 for G–Q when using Qwen3 skills,
and \$2.92 for Q–Q and \$4.96 for G–Q when using Codex skills.

While the Qwen3-Coder Cobot shows a larger improvement in success rate
with the use of skills (Q–Q), the GPT5.2-Codex Cobot (G–G) shows a
smaller increase, though with a more substantial cost reduction. For
GPT5.2-Codex, the success rate increases from 0.93 without skills to
0.97 when using the Qwen3 skill set and to 0.99 when using the Codex
skill set. The reduction in cost is larger, decreasing from \$31.44
without skills to \$28.82 with the Qwen3 skill set and to \$20.44 with
the Codex skill set. A similar trend is observed for the cross-pairing
setting (Q–G), where the GPT5.2-Codex Cobot benefits less from
cross-pairing, with the success rate decreasing and cost remaining
higher. In particular, the cost reaches \$54.62 in the no-skill setting
compared to \$31.44 for G–G. This behavior is largely due to ambiguous
instructions that trigger additional clarification questions, resulting
in longer interactions, increased token usage, and slightly lower
reconstruction success.

These results demonstrate that skills generated during the
reconstruction task are model-agnostic and can be reused by cobots
powered by different models for subsequent tasks resulting in improved
success rates and reduced costs. We next evaluate the applicability of
these reusable skills in the Repeat test.

### 6.3 Repeat

Similar to the reuse task evaluation, the repeat task examines whether
the models can use learned skills to reconstruct boards that contain
repeated placements of the same object across the grid. The experiments
consider three settings: (a) no-skills, where the models perform the
task without access to any learned skills; (b) Qwen3-Coder skills, a
skill set learned by the Qwen3-Coder Cobot; and (c) GPT5.2-Codex skills,
a skill set learned by the GPT5.2-Codex Cobot. The models are evaluated
in both self-play and cross-pairing settings.

Impact of Skill Usage: As shown in
Figure [8](#S6.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 6.3 Repeat ‣ 6 Results ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots"),
the repeat task also shows benefits from the use of learned skills for
the Qwen3-Coder Cobot. In self-play, the success rate increases from
0.46 without skills to 0.73 and 0.70 when using the Qwen3-Coder and
GPT5.2-Codex skill sets respectively, while the cost is reduced from
\$28.37 to \$11.84 and \$12.70. When cross-paired with GPT5.2-Codex as
the Programmer, the success rate increases from 0.89 to 0.93 for both
skill sets, while the cost decreases from \$67.40 to \$27.68 and
\$23.65. The higher cost in the repeat task compared to other tasks is
due to repeated placements of the same object, which lead to multiple
instructions, clarification requests, or corrections, and therefore
increased token usage.

![Refer to caption](2611.00297v1/repeat_stats.png)

Figure 8: Trade-off between token cost and repeat task success rate
across model configurations. Results compare responses generated without
skills, with Qwen skills, and with Codex skills, showing that skill
usage significantly improves success rates while maintaining relatively
low token cost; The y-axis is truncated to the range $`0.4-1.0`$ to
highlight differences among performance scores.

In contrast, the GPT5.2-Codex Cobot shows similar success rates across
the no-skill and skill settings. The success rate changes from 0.98
without skills to 0.97 with the Qwen3-Coder skill set and 0.99 with the
GPT5.2-Codex skill set, while the cost decreases from \$40.67 to \$28.89
and \$19.90 respectively. The decrease in success rate in the
cross-pairing case is due to ambiguous instructions, similar to the
reuse scenarios. This effect is more in the repeat task compared to the
reuse task because the reuse task involves a single object placement,
whereas the repeat task requires placing the same object multiple times
on the grid.

Together, the Reuse and Repeat evaluations show that the skills learned
from Teach and Abstract steps can be Applied to new contexts across
different model configurations. The learned skills are transferable
across models, can improve task performance, and reduce the associated
costs.

Skill retrieval analysis in
Section [6.4.1](#S6.SS4.SSS1 "6.4.1 Skill Retrieval Rate ‣ 6.4 Skill Retrieval Analysis ‣ 6 Results ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots")
shows that the models are able to retrieve most of the skills across
different configurations. However, during a random manual analysis of
skill usage, we observed scenarios, where the model generates a skill
that is not available (the skill was not learned during reconstruction)
in the model context. We refer to these scenarios as skill
hallucinations and analyse their impact on the task success. However,
these are not random hallucinations as the generated function call
follows the correct function signature, with the correct skill name and
relevant arguments. As a design choice, we execute these generated
skills in the virtual simulator using the ground truth function
definition. This choice allows us to isolate and evaluate the Cobot’s
ability to correctly predict skill usage, specifically the correct
object name, colors, locations, regardless of whether the skill exists
in the library.

Table [3](#S6.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 6.4.1 Skill Retrieval Rate ‣ 6.4 Skill Retrieval Analysis ‣ 6 Results ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots")
shows the percentage of hallucinated skills across skill sets and model
configurations. The hallucination percentages are higher when the Qwen
skill set is used, as only 315 skills are available for the 495 test
instances, compared to the Codex skill set, for which 415 skills are
available. We also compute the success rate for these hallucinated
instances and the success rate is $`1.0`$ regardless of the model
configuration, further confirming that the models generally predict
task-relevant skills.

Overall, these results demonstrate that skills generated during the
reconstruction task are model-agnostic and consistently improve task
performance when successfully retrieved. The impact of skill reuse
varies by model: for Qwen3-Coder, skill reuse primarily improves success
rates, while for GPT5.2-Codex, the benefit is more in terms of cost
reduction. Skill retrieval rates are high across all configurations. In
cases where skills are unavailable, models tend to hallucinate skills
that align with the context. Regardless of hallucination, the predicted
skills align with the input context, confirming that the models
generally predict task-relevant skills. When retrieval doesn’t succeed,
the interaction falls back to reconstruction, where success rates vary
considerably across model configurations. We also observe that both
Cobots are sensitive to the choice of Programmer and this has an impact
on retrieval rates. Together, these findings highlight that reliable
skill retrieval and context-aware skill prediction become increasingly
important as task complexity grows.

### 6.5 Qualitative Analysis

Figure 9: Qualitative examples (Q-Q setup) showing clarification and
correction during reconstruction, misinterpretation during skill reuse,
fallback from reuse to reconstruction, and hallucinated skill use. These
showcase how Programmer and Cobot interact across task settings, how
errors arise from ambiguous or incorrect skill selection, and how the
system either continues through correction, falls back to primitive
reconstruction; Q-Q: Qwen3-Coder is used as both Programmer and Cobot.

The qualitative examples in
Figure [9](#S6.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ 6.5 Qualitative Analysis ‣ 6 Results ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots")
highlight different behaviors across the reconstruction and reuse
settings. In reconstruction, the interaction supports clarification and
correction. When Cobot cannot infer the instruction, it asks Programmer
for additional information. Programmer then elaborates the instruction,
and later corrects an error in the generated code by specifying that the
washer should be red. This example shows how the multi-turn setup allows
the task to continue even when the initial instruction is incomplete or
when the generated code contains a mismatch.

The reuse examples show that skill availability alone does not guarantee
correct skill use. In one case, Cobot misinterprets the object
description by treating the two halves of a bridge as separate
components, which leads to an incorrect function call. This suggests
that reuse errors can also arise from Cobot interpretations. In another
case, although the relevant skill is available in the context, Cobot
fails to call it and instead generates primitive code. The interaction
then falls back to the reconstruction loop, where Programmer continues
with step-by-step instructions and corrections.

The reuse scenario also showcases a different failure mode, where Cobot
calls a hallucinated skill that is not present in the available skill
library. However, the generated call still uses the correct colors and
location arguments, indicating that the model can sometimes infer the
intended structure even when it is not available in the context.
Together, these cases suggest that TAA’s multi-turn design helps recover
from ambiguity and local execution errors, while reuse failures often
arise from skill grounding issues, instruction misinterpretation, and
incorrect selection or application of learned skills.

Figure 10: Reuse Task: Clarification behavior under skill reuse settings
as a function of task complexity. (a) Clarification episodes remain
sparse across all model configurations, with occasional increases for
G–Q at higher complexity, while Q–Q and H–Q exhibit minimal
clarification needs overall. (b) Median dialogue turns for successful
instances are nearly constant, with H–Q consistently requiring two
turns, and both Q–Q and G–Q completing interactions in approximately a
single turn. Model Configuration: Q–Q (Qwen3-Coder–Qwen3-Coder), G–Q
(GPT5.2-Codex–Qwen3-Coder), and H–Q (Human–Qwen3-Coder).

Figure 11: Repeat Task: Clarification behavior across model
configuration as a function of task complexity. (a) Number of
clarification episodes increases with the number of elements, with Q–Q
and H–Q showing stronger sensitivity compared to G–Q. (b) Median
dialogue turns for successful instances remain relatively stable, with
H–Q requiring consistently more turns, while G–Q maintains minimal
interaction length across all settings. Model Configuration: Q–Q
(Qwen3-Coder–Qwen3-Coder), G–Q (GPT5.2-Codex–Qwen3-Coder), and H–Q
(Human–Qwen3-Coder).

|                     |       |        |
| ------------------- | ----- | ------ |
| Model Configuration | Reuse | Repeat |
| Human-Q             | 0.96  | 0.94   |
| Q-Q                 | 0.88  | 0.78   |
| G-Q                 | 1.00  | 0.94   |

configurations, including a human baseline for the evaluated subset

### 6.6 Evaluation with a Human Programmer

As mentioned in
Section [5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Evaluation with a Human Programmer ‣ 5 Experimental Setup ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots"),
we randomly selected $`50`$ test instances for the reuse and repeat
tasks and evaluated with one human Programmer as a pilot evaluation.
This evaluation (see
Table [4](#S6.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 6.5 Qualitative Analysis ‣ 6 Results ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots"))
measures the performance of the Apply step when natural language
instructions are provided by a human Programmer and the Cobot is powered
by Qwen3-Coder. Overall, the Cobot is able to interpret human
instructions and achieves comparable success rates to the model-based
Programmer configurations for both the reuse and repeat tasks. The human
Programmer achieves higher success rates than the Qwen3-Coder Programmer
in the same Cobot configuration, suggesting that the Cobot is able to
interpret human instructions effectively.

We analyse the episodes where clarification questions are present and
whether the interaction behavior differs between human and model-based
Programmers.
Figure [10](#S6.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ 6.5 Qualitative Analysis ‣ 6 Results ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots")
plot (a) shows how many episodes contain clarification questions for
each model configuration in the reuse task. Q-Q has only one instance
with a clarification question for a 5-element object, while G-Q has four
instances for 5-element objects. H-Q has one episode each for three and
four element objects. For the repeat task, the number of clarification
episodes is slightly higher, with Q-Q peaking at 10 episodes for
4-element objects. We also analyse the median number of turns for all
successful instances for each configuration. For the reuse task, the
human Programmer consistently takes two turns while model-based
Programmers take one turn. For the repeat task, the human Programmer
takes three turns compared to one turn for model-based Programmers,
suggesting that human instructions require more interaction to complete
successfully.

Although this is a pilot study and the number of test instances are
limited, this evaluation suggests that the pipeline can be extended to
human Programmers, and that the Cobot can retrieve and apply skills even
when instructions are human-written rather than generated by another
model.

## 7 Conclusion

In this work, we propose the Teach-Abstract-Apply (TAA) framework, which
enables users to teach collaborative robots new spatial manipulation
routines through multi-turn natural language dialogue. The framework
defines a three-stage pipeline: Teach, where a user interacts with the
robot and iteratively refines the workflows; Abstract, where the
resulting interaction trace is abstracted into a generalised behavior
(skill); and Apply, where the abstracted skills are applied in different
settings. We then test the TAA framework through a collaborative
structure-building task, in which a Programmer instructs the Cobot to
reconstruct a goal board through dialogue, the resulting interaction is
abstracted into a reusable Python skill function and these abstracted
skills are applied to new scenarios through reuse and repeat tasks. Our
evaluation using both open-weight (Qwen3-Coder) and closed
(GPT5.2-Codex) models in self-play and cross-model configurations on the
SARTCo dataset demonstrates that:

- •
  Abstracted skills are model-agnostic and consistently improve task
  success rates while reducing interaction cost compared to the no-skill
  baseline.
- •
  Skill retrieval rates are high across all configurations, with models
  demonstrating strong context-awareness in identifying and applying
  relevant skills.
- •
  Models tend to hallucinate skills that align with the task context,
  and these hallucinated skills achieve a 1.0 success rate, confirming
  that models correctly predict skill usage even when the exact skill is
  absent from the library.
- •
  The benefit of skill reuse varies by model capability, with smaller
  models benefiting more in terms of success rate improvement and larger
  models benefiting more in terms of cost reduction.
- •
  A preliminary human evaluation suggests that the pipeline also works
  with human instructions without requiring changes to the system.

These findings demonstrate the potential of combining dialogue-based
teaching with program synthesis for scalable, reusable robot skill
learning. Future work will focus on expanding the human evaluation to a
more diverse participant pool, and evaluating the framework on diverse
tasks and modalities. Additionally, incorporating safety mechanisms for
real-world deployment and exploring the integration of TAA with a
physical robot arm remain important directions for future work.

## 8 Limitations

Our proposed TAA framework demonstrates promising results for
dialogue-based robot skill acquisition, but several limitations remain.

Physical Robot: Our proposed setup uses a virtual simulator in a
controlled setting. As a design choice, we did not include the physical
robot in the current setup, as perception, motion planning and low-level
control may introduce additional failures ([Kim et al.,
2026](#bib.bib83)) beyond these associated with TAA components. We view
this as a realistic starting point for evaluating the feasibility of TAA
independently, with the potential to extend it to real-world settings
involving a physical robot.

Evaluation of Skill Quality: The optimizer’s correctness is currently
judged by board state reproduction and structural metrics. While
execution success confirms robustness and structural metrics assess
minimality, the current evaluation does not assess higher-order
properties such as skill composability beyond the reuse and repeat
tasks.

Baselines: The primary comparison is against a no-skill baseline within
the TAA framework. To our knowledge, no existing baseline combines
dialogue-based teaching with persistent skill reuse, making direct
comparison with prior work challenging.

Safety: The current framework operates in a controlled simulation
environment. Scaling to real-world deployment would require additional
safety mechanisms, such as ambiguity detection, formal verification of
generated code, or constrained APIs with whitelisted operations, to
mitigate risks associated with hallucinated skills or ambiguous
instructions.

Dataset Scale: The experiments are conducted on the SARTCo dataset,
which covers a specific grid-world environment. Evaluating TAA on larger
and more diverse datasets with varied object types, spatial
configurations, and task complexities would strengthen the
generalizability of the findings.

Model Dependence: The results show that the benefit of skill reuse
depends on the underlying model. Smaller open-weight models such as
Qwen3-Coder benefit more in terms of success rate improvement, while
larger closed models such as GPT5.2-Codex benefit more in terms of cost
reduction. This suggests that the framework’s effectiveness may vary
with model capability.

Human Evaluation Scale: The human-in-the-loop evaluation was conducted
as a pilot study with a single participant, limiting the statistical
generalizability of the findings. A broader user study with a larger and
more diverse participant pool, incorporating objective measures such as
turns-to-success, clarification rates, and task completion time, remains
an important direction for future work.

## 9 Appendix

### 9.1 Interaction Framework

As mentioned in
Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Realising TAA Framework ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots")
of the main content, the TAA interaction framework follows the
clem:todd ([Kranti et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)) player interaction. The
Game Master orchestrates the interaction between both players: the
Programmer and the Cobot. Both players are text-based LLMs. In
self-play, the same LLM plays the roles of both the Programmer and the
Robot, while in cross-play, different models are used as the Programmer
and the Robot. While the Programmer is instructed to respond with the
follow-up instruction in string format, the Robot is instructed to
respond with a JSON object containing the keys status and details. The
status can have the values code, clarification, or acknowledgement. The
details will vary depending on the status. If the status is code, the
details will contain executable code, or a string if it is clarification
or acknowledgement. The Game Master receives the information from each
player, strips off the anchors, and routes the response to the next
step. In the case of a Robot response, it also validates whether the
expected structure is followed, i.e., whether the status and details
keys exist and hold only the expected values. If the status is code, the
Game Master passes the player-generated code to the virtual simulator
for execution, and if it is clarification or acknowledgement, it passes
the response to the Programmer. If there are any errors in the code
execution, the error feedback is passed to the Robot. The Robot may
either correct the code or chose to ask for clarification from the
Programmer if there are any ambiguities.

#### 9.1.1 Virtual Simulator

The virtual simulator is used to execute the Robot-generated code to
update the placement of components in the grid-based environment. As
mentioned in
Section [4](#S4 "4 Methodology ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots")
of the main content, the grid-based environment uses a 2.5D grid of size
8x8, where each grid cell allows component placement and stacking. If
the code execution is successful, the resultant world is returned with
cell-by-cell stacking details to the Game Master, which are then added
to the Programmer’s prompt in the next turn. If there are failures
during execution, the error information is passed to the Robot for
further processing.

### 9.2 Prompt Structure

We follow the standard ([Brown et al., 2020](#bib.bib84); [Wei et al.,
2022](#bib.bib85); [Liu et al., 2023](#bib.bib86)) prompting approaches
to structure our Programmer and Cobot prompts. Both players are prompted
in zero-shot settings. Each prompt consists of a system message, task
description, environment information along with the constraints,
followed by the expected response structure and the dialogue history up
to that turn. Additionally, Programmer’s prompt consists the difference
board (i.e., the cell-level differences between the goal board and the
Robot’s reconstructed board) which can guide the Programmer in
generating the follow-up instruction. In order to ensure consistent
boundaries for the model inputs and outputs, we added response anchors
(inspired by DSPy ([Khattab et al., 2023](#bib.bib2))) \[\[ \## prompt
\## \]\] and \[\[ \## completed \## \]\] at the beginning and end of
each prompt. The interaction will be aborted if any of the players’
responses do not follow the response constraints and will continue until
the Programmer responds with DONE or the maximum number of turns
($`15`$) is reached. More details about the prompt ablation studies are
available in the supplementary material.

### 9.3 Prompt Ablation Studies

We conducted multiple experiments to refine the prompt templates and
response constraints. We began by varying the number of turns required
for the interaction from $`1`$ to $`20`$ and, based on the results (see
Table [5](#S9.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 9.3 Prompt Ablation Studies ‣ 9 Appendix ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots")),
fixed it at $`15`$ turns. We then continued the ablations for the number
of optimization turns and retry turns and chose $`10`$ and $`3`$,
respectively, based on the results (see
Tables [6](#S9.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 9.3 Prompt Ablation Studies ‣ 9 Appendix ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots")
and [7](#S9.T7 "Table 7 ‣ 9.3 Prompt Ablation Studies ‣ 9 Appendix ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots")).
The next set of ablations focused on the necessity of including the
difference grid, error feedback, and clarification questions.
Table [8](#S9.T8 "Table 8 ‣ 9.3 Prompt Ablation Studies ‣ 9 Appendix ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots")
shows that the success rate decreased when these were not included in
the prompt, and hence we retained them in the final prompt structure.
Figures [12](#S9.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ 9.3 Prompt Ablation Studies ‣ 9 Appendix ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots")-to-[30](#S9.F30 "Figure 30 ‣ 9.3 Prompt Ablation Studies ‣ 9 Appendix ‣ Teach, Abstract, Apply: A Framework for Dialogue-Driven Task Learning with Collaborative Robots")
shows the prompt structure used across the experiments for both the
players.

| --------- | ---------- | ------------ | ------------ |
| Ablations | Abort Rate | Failure Rate | Success Rate |
| n=1       | 0.013      | 0.642        | 0.345        |
| n=3       | 0.006      | 0.558        | 0.436        |
| n=5       | 0.006      | 0.448        | 0.545        |
| n=10      | 0.012      | 0.424        | 0.564        |
| n=15      | 0.0        | 0.382        | 0.618        |
| n=20      | 0.0        | 0.380        | 0.620        |
